tagline: A medieval capital on the Baltic's busiest sea corridor — where the fast way to Helsinki, and to your own island suburbs, is the water.
summary: Tallinn is a compact Baltic capital wrapped around the Gulf of Finland, with island and peninsula suburbs — Viimsi, Kakumäe, Aegna, Naissaar, Prangli — that are minutes apart by water but long road loops by car. It is also the southern terminus of the busiest international passenger-sea corridor in the Baltic, the Tallinn–Helsinki crossing, where multiple operators move millions of passengers a year on large diesel ferries. Between the slow island ferries and the heavy cross-gulf boats sits an open lane for a clean, fast, on-demand foiling tier — and Bolt, an Estonian company headquartered in Tallinn, is the natural brand to run it on its home water.
competitive_landscape: Today the water splits into two unconnected worlds: high-volume diesel car-ferries on the Tallinn–Helsinki trunk (Tallink, Viking Line, Eckerö), and small municipal island ferries to Aegna, Naissaar and Prangli that run a handful of sailings a day. Neither is fast, on-demand, or premium. There is no foiling, zero-emission, app-hailed layer linking the city's own marinas and island suburbs — and Bolt already owns the urban mobility relationship in its hometown. That gap, on home turf, is the opening.

demand_signals.label: Tallinn–Helsinki sea corridor
demand_signals.note: One of the busiest international passenger-ferry routes in Europe, with several million crossings a year on the ~43 nm Gulf of Finland link — a proven, dense cross-water travel market.

demand_signals.label: Island & peninsula suburbs
demand_signals.note: Viimsi, Kakumäe, Aegna, Naissaar and Prangli are close by sea but slow by the long road loops around the bays — classic foiling shortcut geography.
demand_signals.value: Aegna ~7 nm · Naissaar ~11 nm · Prangli ~5 nm

demand_signals.label: Old Town cruise & visitor volume
demand_signals.note: Tallinn's UNESCO Old Town draws heavy Baltic-cruise and short-break tourism that arrives by sea and moves to marinas, Pirita and the islands.

journeys.today: A road loop around the bay through city traffic to the Olympic marina.
journeys.with_navier: A direct ~4.5 nm all-electric foiling hop from the cruise quay to Pirita — minutes, silent, low-wash.

journeys.today: A long peninsular drive around Tallinn Bay at peak.
journeys.with_navier: A short cross-bay foiling shuttle that turns a congested commute into a few clean minutes.

journeys.today: A ~2-hour diesel car-ferry on a fixed timetable across the Gulf of Finland.
journeys.with_navier: A faster, smoother Quanta-LR hybrid crossing on the Baltic's busiest sea corridor — premium, on-demand, no charging dependency mid-gulf.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The city-and-island mesh — Old City Harbour↔Pirita (~4.5 nm), Tallinn↔Viimsi/Kakumäe (~5–6 nm), Aegna (~7 nm), Naissaar (~11 nm), Prangli (~5 nm) — all sits well inside the 70 nm all-electric envelope, ideal for high-frequency clean rotations off existing harbour and marina berths.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: The Tallinn↔Helsinki crossing (~43 nm) is comfortably foilable, but the long Baltic trunks beyond — Tallinn↔Stockholm (~210 nm) — are Quanta-LR hybrid corridors (H2 2026+); the hybrid range removes any mid-Baltic charging dependency and opens line-haul no all-electric day-boat can serve.

precedents.what: Electric hydrofoil passenger service (Candela P-12) entering scheduled city water-transport use in the Stockholm archipelago
precedents.why_it_matters: A directly comparable Nordic capital proving foiling craft as a clean, fast public-water-transport tier — the same Baltic operating context Tallinn shares.

regulatory_note: Maritime activity is overseen by the Estonian Transport Administration (Transpordiamet) and the Port of Tallinn; island services fall under municipal transport. The Tallinn–Helsinki corridor is an intra-Schengen EU crossing, simplifying cross-border operation. Estonia's strong digital-state and clean-tech posture aligns with an all-electric, app-hailed fleet, and Bolt's home-market standing eases the permitting conversation.
seasonality: A summer-weighted market (May–September) for island and leisure runs, when the gulf is calm and long daylight extends operating hours; the Tallinn–Helsinki commuter and freight corridor runs year-round, with winter ice and storms the main disruption window where reliability is most valued.
